sections.heading: What training on examples actually does
Moving work to a smaller model

slides.title: Adapters and *fine-tuning*
slides.text: What does training on examples change, and what can it not do?

narration: This video is about the first change that touches the model itself.
You teach it with examples of the task done well.

slides.caption: The first change to the model itself. You teach it with examples of the task done well.

slides.title: What we will *cover*
items: Moving work to a smaller model

narration: This video covers adapters and fine-tuning.
The first three steps of the ladder change the system around the model.
The model itself stays the same.
This is the first option that changes the model itself.
First, we look at what training on examples really does.
Then we see three ways to do it and what you need before you start.
Next, we see how to move work to a smaller model.
Last comes the test for moving on.

slides.caption: The first option that changes the model itself. How training on examples works, three ways to do it, what you need, and when to move on.

slides.title: Teach the model with *examples*
slides.text: Each example shows an input and the answer you want.
slides.picture: A stack of paired question and answer cards feeding into a small device.

narration: Until now, the model itself stayed the same.
Now you change it.
You collect many examples of the task done well.
Each example is an input paired with the answer you wanted.
The model is trained on these pairs until it answers more like them.
Each example shows the model the right answer to aim for.
Training a model this way is called supervised fine-tuning.
From here on, we will just say fine-tuning.

slides.caption: Supervised fine-tuning trains a model on examples of a task done well. Each example pairs an input with the answer you wanted.

slides.title: What fine-tuning is *for*

left.head: Right tool for
rows: Moving work to a smaller model

narration: Fine-tuning is the right tool for two jobs.
It makes the model behave the same way every time.
And it can move work to a smaller, cheaper model.
It is the wrong tool for teaching the model facts.
The next slides show why.

slides.caption: Fine-tuning makes behaviour consistent and moves work to smaller, cheaper models. It does not teach facts.

slides.title: How training on *examples* works

narration: To see why, look at what training does inside the model.
A model is a huge set of numbers.
These numbers are called weights.
Training shows the model an input and the answer you wanted.
It measures how far the model's own answer is from that.
Then it nudges the weights a little to close the gap.
This repeats over thousands of examples.
Slowly, the model's usual behaviour moves toward the pattern the examples share.

slides.caption: Fine-tuning compares the model's answer with the wanted answer. It nudges the weights slightly to close the gap. Over thousands of examples, the usual behaviour shifts.

slides.title: It learns the *shape* of answers
slides.text: The facts behind the examples are not stored.
slides.picture: A stencil copying a page layout onto a sheet, with the boxes left empty.

narration: Training rewards answers that look like your examples.
So the model learns their structure, their tone and their confidence.
Nothing in the process stores the facts behind them.
A few thousand examples cannot carry a million facts.
So a fine-tuned model can sound just like your examples and still get details wrong.

slides.caption: Training rewards answers shaped like the examples. It teaches the style and the confidence. It does not store the facts.

slides.title: Facts stay out of the *weights*

narration: So where should facts come from?
Look them up at the moment the model needs them.
Then pass them to the model with the question.
This is called retrieval.
Facts baked into the weights cannot be traced back to a source.
They cannot be updated or deleted either.
Facts that are looked up can be traced, updated and deleted.

slides.caption: Facts should be looked up when needed. Facts in the weights cannot be traced, updated or deleted. Facts that are looked up can.

slides.title: It can *forget* other skills
slides.text: It is a side effect of how training works.
slides.picture: A device taking in a new block while older blocks fall away.

narration: Fine-tuning also has a side effect.
The weights being nudged also hold the model's general skills.
If you push them hard toward your task, they drift.
The model can lose skills it had before.
This is called catastrophic forgetting.

slides.caption: The weights that learn your task also hold general skills. Catastrophic forgetting comes from how training works. It is not a sign of careless work.

slides.title: Full fine-tuning changes *every* weight

narration: Now for how fine-tuning is actually done.
There are three main ways.
The first changes every weight in the model.
This is called full fine-tuning.
It has the most power to change behaviour.
It also needs the most computing power.
And you end up with a whole new model to store and run.

slides.caption: Full fine-tuning changes all the weights. It can change behaviour the most and needs the most computing power. The result is a whole model to run.

slides.title: LoRA trains a small *add-on*
slides.picture: A large locked block with two thin strips beside it. Only the strips are trained.

narration: The second way leaves the model's own weights locked.
The change fine-tuning makes can usually be captured in two small tables of numbers.
So only those two small tables are trained.
When the model runs, their effect is added on top.
This method is called LoRA.

slides.caption: LoRA locks the model's own weights. It trains two small tables of numbers beside them. Their effect is added when the model runs.

slides.title: Adapters you can *swap*
slides.text: One shared model, a different adapter per task.
slides.picture: One large block with small cards beside it, and one card plugged in.

narration: A whole model takes gigabytes of space.
What LoRA produces takes only megabytes.
This small add-on is called an adapter.
You can keep one shared model running.
Then you swap in a different adapter for each task.
So one model can do many different jobs.

slides.caption: LoRA produces an adapter of megabytes, not a model of gigabytes. One shared model can swap in a different adapter for each task.

slides.title: QLoRA *compresses* the locked model
slides.text: One powerful chip can adapt a large model.
slides.picture: A large locked block squeezed flat by a clamp, with a thin strip on top.

narration: The third way builds on LoRA.
While the adapter trains, the locked model is stored in a compressed form.
That saves so much computer memory that one powerful chip can adapt a large model.
The adapter itself is not compressed.
The quality stays close to LoRA.
This method is called QLoRA.

slides.caption: QLoRA compresses the locked model during training. The adapter itself is not compressed. Quality is close to LoRA on far less hardware.

slides.title: Adapters do not prevent *forgetting*
slides.text: If forgetting matters for your use, measure it.

narration: Changing fewer weights sounds safer.
You might expect an adapter to protect the model's other skills.
But published research found that LoRA does not protect them.
If forgetting matters for your use, measure it.

slides.caption: Changing fewer weights sounds safer. Published research found that LoRA does not protect general skills. The repair for forgetting is covered under distillation.

slides.title: When fine-tuning *fits*
items: Examples in instructions did not help
slides.picture: Three correct answer sheets, each laid out in a different order.

narration: Whichever way you choose, first check that fine-tuning fits your problem.
Here is the typical case.
The answers are already correct.
But their structure and tone still vary from one answer to the next.
Adding example answers to the instructions has not fixed it.

slides.caption: The answers are correct. Their structure and tone still vary. Examples in the instructions have not fixed it. That is the fine-tuning use case.

slides.title: What you need *before* starting
items: A plan to run the result

narration: You need a few thousand examples.
The model learns exactly what they teach.
That includes their mistakes.
So their quality matters more than anything else.
Before training, write a set of tests and lock them.
Include tests for skills that should not change.
If you only test the new task, forgetting can slip through unnoticed.
You also need a plan to run the result.
An adapter needs its original model to run on.
When that model is replaced, the work must be redone and tested again.

slides.caption: A small careful set of examples beats a large scraped one. Testing only the new task lets forgetting slip through unnoticed.

slides.title: Someone else can run the *training*
slides.text: A provider runs fine-tuning for you as a service.

narration: The training itself has to happen somewhere.
You do not have to use your own machines.
Some providers run fine-tuning for you as a service.
This is called a managed option.
You send the examples and get back the trained result.

slides.caption: A managed option is a service that runs fine-tuning for you. You send the examples and get back the result.

slides.title: The managed options *narrowed* in 2026
slides.source: OpenAI deprecations page, announced 7 May 2026, as of August 2026

narration: These managed options changed in 2026.
This fact changes often.
It is correct as of August 2026.
OpenAI is closing the fine-tuning that customers set up themselves.
It is closing in stages.
Remaining customers can start no new jobs after 6 January 2027.
Managed fine-tuning on the major cloud platforms is still available.
Some models let you download their weights and run them yourself.
These are called open-weight models.
Adapters on these models are unaffected.

slides.caption: As of August 2026. For most companies the OpenAI route is already closed. Existing fine-tuned models keep running until their original models retire.

slides.title: Move the work to a *small model*
slides.text: A small model on your own servers can cost far less.
slides.picture: A folder moving from a very large device to a small one.

narration: Now back to one of the two jobs fine-tuning is good for.
The biggest and most capable models cost the most to run.
These are called frontier models.
Fine-tuning can move a task from a frontier model to a small one.
A small fine-tuned model can do the task for a fraction of the cost.
It can run on your own servers.
Your data then stays with you.

slides.caption: A small model with an adapter on your own servers can do the task at a fraction of the cost. The data stays inside.

slides.title: One test is one *data point*
slides.text: Prove it on your own tests before you switch.

narration: One published test compared a small fine-tuned model with a frontier model.
The frontier model was given careful instructions instead.
The task was putting items into the right category.
The small model won by a wide margin at far lower cost.
But that is only one test.
Prove it on your own tests before you switch.

slides.caption: One published test on a sorting task. A small fine-tuned model beat a frontier model with careful instructions. It cost a fraction as much.

slides.title: The test for *moving on*
slides.text: Format and behaviour are fixed. What is wrong is judgement or knowledge.

narration: So when is this step done?
Move on when the format and behaviour of the answers are right.
At that point, what is still wrong is judgement or knowledge.
Where you go next depends on which one it is.

slides.caption: Adapters have closed the format and behaviour gap. What remains wrong is judgement or knowledge. The next step depends on the symptom.

slides.title: Wrong *judgement*
items: Reasoning wrong, outcome can be graded

narration: Say the answers look right, but the reasoning is wrong.
And say a program can check whether each outcome is right.
Then go to reinforcement fine-tuning.
There, the model tries the task and learns from the scores it gets.

slides.caption: The shape is right, but the reasoning is wrong on outcomes a program can grade. Go to reinforcement fine-tuning.

slides.title: Misreads your *field*

narration: Say the model still misreads the language and documents of your field.
Then go to continued pretraining.
There, the model keeps learning from large amounts of your own text.

slides.caption: The model still misreads the language and documents of your field. Go to continued pretraining.

slides.title: Right quality, too *costly*
items: Quality right, cost or speed wrong

narration: Say the quality is right, but it costs too much or runs too slowly.
Then go to distillation.
There, a large model trains a small one to do the same work.

slides.caption: Quality is right. Cost or speed is the complaint. Go to distillation.

slides.title: What to *remember*
items: It can make a model forget
Small models can take over work

narration: Fine-tuning trains a model on examples of a task done well.
It makes behaviour consistent.
It does not teach the model facts.
Facts should still be looked up when the model needs them.
Training can make the model forget other skills.
Adapters do not stop this.
So measure it.
An adapter is a small add-on you can swap for each task.
Fine-tuning can also move work to a smaller, cheaper model.
Next up is distillation.

slides.caption: Fine-tuning teaches behaviour, not facts. Facts should be looked up. Training can cause forgetting. Adapters are small and swappable. It can move work to smaller models.
